title: Predicting the impact of patient and private provider behavior on diagnostic delay for pulmonary tuberculosis patients in India: A simulation modeling study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) incidence in India continues to be high due, in large part, to long delays experienced by patients before successful diagnosis and treatment initiation, especially in the private sector. This diagnostic delay is driven by patients' inclination to switch between different types of providers and providers' inclination to delay ordering of accurate diagnostic tests relevant to TB. Our objective is to quantify the impact of changes in these behavioral characteristics of providers and patients on diagnostic delay experienced by pulmonary TB patients. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We developed a discrete event simulation model of patients' diagnostic pathways that captures key behavioral characteristics of providers (time to order a test) and patients (time to switch to another provider). We used an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate the parameters underlying these behavioral characteristics, with quantitative data encoded from detailed interviews of 76 and 64 pulmonary TB patients in the 2 Indian cities of Mumbai and Patna, respectively, which were conducted between April and August 2014. We employed the estimated model to simulate different counterfactual scenarios of diagnostic pathways under altered behavioral characteristics of providers and patients to predict their potential impact on the diagnostic delay. Private healthcare providers including chemists were the first point of contact for the majority of TB patients in Mumbai (70%) and Patna (94%). In Mumbai, 45% of TB patients first approached less-than-fully-qualified providers (LTFQs), who take 28.71 days on average for diagnosis. About 61% of these patients switched to other providers without a diagnosis. Our model estimates that immediate testing for TB by LTFQs at the first visit (at the current level of diagnostic accuracy) could reduce the average diagnostic delay from 35.53 days (95% CI: 34.60, 36.46) to 18.72 days (95% CI: 18.01, 19.43). In Patna, 61% of TB patients first approached fully qualified providers (FQs), who take 9.74 days on average for diagnosis. Similarly, immediate testing by FQs at the first visit (at the current level of diagnostic accuracy) could reduce the average diagnostic delay from 23.39 days (95% CI: 22.77, 24.02) to 11.16 days (95% CI: 10.52, 11.81). Improving the diagnostic accuracy of providers per se, without reducing the time to testing, was not predicted to lead to any reduction in diagnostic delay. Our study was limited because of its restricted geographic scope, small sample size, and possible recall bias, which are typically associated with studies of patient pathways using patient interviews. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, we found that encouraging private providers to order definitive TB diagnostic tests earlier during patient consultation may have substantial impact on reducing diagnostic delay in these urban Indian settings. These results should be combined with disease transmission models to predict the impact of changes in provider behavior on TB incidence.

summary.oneLiner: Simulation of TB patient pathways in Mumbai and Patna suggests earlier test ordering by providers could cut diagnostic delay far more than improving their accuracy.
summary.overview: Tuberculosis patients in two Indian cities often first visit private providers, including less-than-fully-qualified providers and chemists, and then switch between providers before being diagnosed, which prolongs diagnostic delay. The authors built a discrete event simulation (a computer model that runs many virtual patient journeys) calibrated on interviews with 76 Mumbai and 64 Patna patients. They tested counterfactual scenarios in which providers order TB tests earlier or become more accurate. The model suggests that earlier test ordering could substantially reduce delay, while higher accuracy alone was not predicted to reduce it.
summary.question: How do patient switching behavior and provider timing of diagnostic test ordering, along with provider diagnostic accuracy, affect diagnostic delay for pulmonary tuberculosis patients in India?
summary.method: A discrete event simulation model of patient diagnostic pathways, with parameters estimated using an expectation-maximization algorithm. The authors ran counterfactual scenarios that reduced time to diagnosis or raised diagnostic accuracy for less-than-fully-qualified providers (LTFQs) and fully qualified providers (FQs), at provider coverage levels from 20% to 100%, and validated the model against the raw data.
summary.data: Retrospective, population-based household survey data from 2 Indian cities: 76 self-reported pulmonary TB patients in Mumbai and 64 in Patna, interviewed for 60-90 minutes between April and August 2014. Interviews were conducted in 2014 (the paper states the interview period).
findings: In Mumbai, 45% of TB patients first approached LTFQs, who take 28.71 days on average for diagnosis; about 61% of these patients switched to other providers without a diagnosis.
Immediate testing by LTFQs at the first visit, at the current level of accuracy, was estimated to reduce average diagnostic delay in Mumbai from 35.53 days to 18.72 days.
In Patna, 61% of patients first approached FQs, who take 9.74 days on average for diagnosis; immediate testing by FQs was estimated to reduce average delay from 23.39 days to 11.16 days.
Improving provider diagnostic accuracy without reducing time to testing was not predicted to reduce diagnostic delay; the authors say this difference was statistically significant.

The authors describe the shorter time to patient switching at LTFQs as suggestive of lower willingness to remain in care there, while noting they cannot directly estimate this willingness with their data.

The authors suggest that more accurate diagnostic technologies such as GeneXpert might have limited impact on diagnostic delay and TB incidence, based on the high accuracy of FQs and public providers.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest policymakers and implementing agencies should encourage early test ordering by private providers to reduce diagnostic delay and, consequently, disease transmission. They also suggest that recent efforts incentivising FQs to order accurate tests should be complemented with early screening tests and referrals by LTFQs in Mumbai, and that locally optimised strategies may be more effective than a single national intervention. The authors note that the results should be combined with transmission models before drawing conclusions about TB incidence.
